lesson.title: Fahrrad statt Auto
lesson.subtitle: Tom's car breaks down, and a borrowed bicycle changes his mind
lesson.label: s3

hook.title: Before You Read
hook.content: This story is built on comparisons: faster than, slower than, almost as fast. Watch the words als and wie — they are the hinges. The plot is simple: a car stops working, a friend lends a bicycle, and Tom discovers something.

footnotes.title: Benzin & kaputt
footnotes.content: das Benzin = petrol/gas; kaputt = broken. Both are glossed here because the story needs them and they are not in the lesson's word bank.

footnotes.title: ein paar
footnotes.content: ein paar Minuten = a few minutes. Do not confuse it with das Paar (a pair); the small p is the quantity word.

footnotes.title: als vs. wie
footnotes.content: schneller als = faster than; gleich schnell wie = as fast as. German separates the two jobs that English 'as/than' also keeps apart.

pattern.title: Die Geschichte
pattern.content:
Tom ist Bäcker. Er arbeitet in einer kleinen Bäckerei in der Stadt. Eigentlich fährt er jeden Tag mit dem Auto zur Arbeit. Aber das Benzin ist sehr teuer, und sein Auto ist alt.

Heute ist das Auto kaputt. Tom weiß nicht, was er machen soll. Da kommt sein Freund Alex. „Ich kann dir mein Fahrrad geben“, sagt Alex.

Tom setzt sich auf das Fahrrad und fährt zur Bäckerei. Das geht schneller als mit dem Auto! Er ist nur ein paar Minuten langsamer. Am Nachmittag fährt Tom mit dem Rad zurück.

„Danke, Alex! Ich kaufe mir auch ein Fahrrad. Mit dem Fahrrad bin ich fast gleich schnell. Außerdem ist es gut für meine Gesundheit.“

Alex lacht. „Super! Dann machen wir zusammen eine Fahrt.“

exercises.prompt: Reading check — match each story sentence with its English meaning:

matching_pairs.english: Normally Tom drives to work by car every day.
matching_pairs.german: Eigentlich fährt er jeden Tag mit dem Auto zur Arbeit.

matching_pairs.english: But the gas is very expensive.
matching_pairs.german: Aber das Benzin ist sehr teuer.

matching_pairs.english: That is faster than by car.
matching_pairs.german: Das geht schneller als mit dem Auto.

matching_pairs.english: By bike I am almost as fast.
matching_pairs.german: Mit dem Fahrrad bin ich fast gleich schnell.

exercises.target_answer: Eigentlich fährt er jeden Tag mit dem Auto zur Arbeit., Aber das Benzin ist sehr teuer., Heute ist das Auto kaputt., Alex gibt Tom sein Fahrrad., Das geht schneller als mit dem Auto., Mit dem Fahrrad bin ich fast gleich schnell.
exercises.meaning: the story beats: the car, the cost, the breakdown, the borrowed bike, the comparison
exercises.explanation: The middle two sentences are the turn: the car fails, and the bicycle arrives. The last two are Tom's conclusion.

exercises.prompt: Why does Tom not drive today?
exercises.meaning: The car is broken, so Tom cannot drive it.
exercises.explanation: Heute ist das Auto kaputt is the direct cause. The expensive gas is background, not today's problem.

exercises.prompt: How does Tom feel about the bike ride?
options: Surprised that it is almost as fast
exercises.target_answer: Surprised that it is almost as fast
exercises.meaning: Tom is surprised: the bicycle is almost as fast as his car.
exercises.explanation: Das geht schneller als mit dem Auto! and fast gleich schnell show surprise and a changed opinion.

exercises.prompt: What does Tom decide at the end?
options: He wants to buy a bicycle.
He wants to buy a new car.
He wants to sell his bakery.
exercises.target_answer: He wants to buy a bicycle.
exercises.meaning: Tom decides to buy his own bicycle.
exercises.explanation: Ich kaufe mir auch ein Fahrrad is his decision. The health and money reasons support it.

exercises.prompt: Render the thought in German: 'He drives with the bicycle into the city.'
exercises.idea: He drives with the bicycle into the city.
cues: Start with Er fährt — the verb stays in second position.
mit dem Fahrrad is the means of transport.
The destination uses in + accusative: in die Stadt.
exercises.target_answer: Er fährt mit dem Fahrrad in die Stadt
exercises.meaning: He drives with the bicycle into the city.
exercises.explanation: Er fährt ... in die Stadt: the verb is second, the means is mit dem Fahrrad, and the destination is in die Stadt (motion → accusative).

twist.prompt: Without looking back — say in German: 'With the bicycle I am almost as fast.'
twist.target_answer: Mit dem Fahrrad bin ich fast gleich schnell
twist.explanation: Fronting mit dem Fahrrad pulls the verb bin into second position: Mit dem Fahrrad bin ich ... The comparison stays fast gleich schnell.

summary.outcome: Read a comparison-driven story and answer cause, opinion, and decision questions.

use_example.german: Das geht schneller als mit dem Auto, und es ist gut für meine Gesundheit.
use_example.english: That is faster than by car, and it is good for my health.

summary.takeaway: Comparisons carry a story's argument: schneller als, langsamer als, gleich schnell wie. Find the hinge word and you find the claim.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: a birthday, a broken bus, and a very wet arrival.

rad.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *raþą, from the PIE root *Hret- (to roll) - the same root that gave Latin rota and English rotary. [wiktionary]

fahrrad.etymology_derivation: fahren (to drive, the fare root) + Rad (wheel): the driving-wheel. [wiktionary]

auto.etymology_derivation: Short for Automobil — the same Greek autos ('self') loan as English auto, clipped German-style. [wiktionary]

teuer.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *diurijaz — the true twin of English dear (d → t). [wiktionary]

schnell.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German snel, Proto-Germanic *snellaz, meaning quick and bold; the exact English cognate is the rare word snell, still heard in northern England and Scotland. [wiktionary]

langsam.etymology_derivation: Built exactly like English longsome: lang (long) + the suffix -sam, from Proto-West Germanic *langasam. English lost longsome, but the pieces and the pattern are identical. [wiktionary]

gleich.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *galīkaz, having the same form, built from ga- plus the ancestor of -like; the English twin is alike, and the suffix inside it is the same element as English -like and -ly. [wiktionary]

gesundheit.context_translation: Health is more important than money.
gesundheit.etymology_derivation: Gesund (healthy) plus -heit (-ness); the page documents gesund as cognate with English sound — the old healthy-word alive in English in of sound mind. [wiktionary]

bäckerei.etymology_derivation: Bäcker (baker, from backen — English bake) + -ei, the place suffix: the bake-house. [wiktionary]

bäcker.etymology_derivation: Agent noun of backen (bake) + -er, Proto-Germanic *bakārijaz — the direct twin of English baker. [wiktionary]

stadt.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *stadiz — the twin of stead (homestead, instead); final d devoiced to [t]. [wiktionary]

freund.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *frijōndz, 'the loving one' — the exact twin of English friend. [wiktionary]

danke.etymology_derivation: Ellipsis of ich danke dir — the same danken already known (the think/thank family, th→d). [wiktionary]

minute.etymology_derivation: Medieval Latin minūta — the same Latin loan as English minute. [wiktionary]

stunde.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *stundu — cognate with archaic English stound 'hour'. [wiktionary]

geld.context_translation: I have no money with me.
geld.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *geldą 'reward, payment' — kin to English geld and yield, NOT to gold. [wiktionary]

zug.etymology_derivation: Noun of ziehen (to pull — the tow/tug family): a train is 'the pull(er)', an elevator the Aufzug ('up-pull'). [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
